questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish enterprise-scale defense in depth from defense in depth as taught earlier in this path?
options: It doesn't differ at all — stacking more tools on one application is sufficient at any scale
Enterprise-scale defense in depth layers controls across a federation of business units, subsidiaries, and acquired companies, not just around one system
At enterprise scale, defense in depth means removing all network segmentation to simplify management
Enterprise-scale defense in depth applies only to a single flagship application, ignoring every other business unit
questions.explain: Earlier defense in depth layered controls around one system; at true enterprise scale, the thing being defended is a federation of business units, and the layering has to span that whole federation.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a SOC that can only see one business unit is a real liability at enterprise scale?
options: Because single-unit SOCs are always more expensive to staff than centralized ones
Because it violates a specific named compliance framework in every jurisdiction
Because it's blind to an attacker who compromises one business unit and pivots laterally into another — the pattern that matters most at this scale
Because a single-unit SOC cannot legally retain log data for more than 30 days
questions.explain: A siloed SOC can't see cross-business-unit lateral movement, which is exactly the attack pattern enterprise-scale detection has to be designed to catch.

questions.q: What does this lesson say the 2013 Target breach actually illustrates?
options: A segmentation failure between a vendor-facing business function and the payment-card environment, not simply a missing patch
That defense in depth is ineffective at any scale and should be abandoned
That third-party vendors should never be granted any network access under any circumstances
A failure caused entirely by a single unpatched operating system vulnerability
questions.explain: Attackers used third-party HVAC vendor credentials to move from a vendor-management segment into point-of-sale and cardholder-data systems — the individual controls existed, but the segmentation between those business functions didn't actually isolate them.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the enterprise-wide layers this lesson identifies as needing coordination across business units?
options: Identity (a central IdP, SSO, and conditional access)
Governance (a shared minimum baseline plus a tracked exception process)
Endpoint (one EDR/XDR baseline fleet-wide)
Marketing campaign scheduling across business units
questions.explain: The lesson's enterprise-wide layers are identity, network, data, endpoint, detection/response, and governance — marketing scheduling is not a security control layer.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend a centralized minimum baseline with a tracked exception process, rather than forcing identical controls on every business unit?
options: Because exception processes eliminate the need for any baseline at all

Because legacy systems, differing budgets, and differing regulatory obligations make identical timelines impractical, and a documented, owned, time-bound exception keeps the baseline honest instead of becoming unenforced
Because business units should be allowed to ignore the baseline indefinitely with no documentation
Because forcing identical controls everywhere is always cheaper than any exception process
questions.explain: A federated enterprise can't realistically force identical controls on every unit given legacy systems and differing constraints; a tracked, owned, time-bound exception process keeps the baseline meaningful rather than becoming a document nobody follows.
